{{short description|Study of geometric properties of sets through measure theory}}
In [[mathematics]], '''geometric measure theory''' ('''GMT''') is the study of [[geometry|geometric]] properties of [[Set (mathematics)|sets]] (typically in [[Euclidean space]]) through [[measure (mathematics)|measure theory]]. It allows mathematicians to extend tools from [[differential geometry]] to a much larger class of [[Surface (topology)|surface]]s that are not necessarily [[Differentiable manifold|smooth]].

== History ==

Geometric measure theory was born out of the desire to solve [[Plateau's problem]] (named after [[Joseph Plateau]]) which asks if for every smooth closed curve in <math>\mathbb{R}^3</math> there exists a [[Surface (topology)|surface]] of least [[area]] among all surfaces whose [[Boundary (topology)|boundary]] equals the given curve. Such surfaces mimic [[soap film]]s.

The problem had remained open since it was posed in 1760 by [[Joseph Louis Lagrange|Lagrange]]. It was solved independently in the 1930s by [[Jesse Douglas]] and [[Tibor Radó]] under certain [[topology|topological]] restrictions. In 1960 [[Herbert Federer]] and [[Wendell Fleming]] used the theory of [[Current (mathematics)|currents]] with which they were able to solve the orientable Plateau's problem [[Mathematical Analysis|analytically]] without topological restrictions, thus sparking geometric measure theory. Later [[Jean Taylor]] after [[Frederick J. Almgren, Jr.|Fred Almgren]] proved [[Plateau's laws]] for the kind of singularities that can occur in these more general soap films and soap bubbles clusters.

== Important notions ==

The following objects are central in geometric measure theory:
* [[Hausdorff measure]] and [[Hausdorff dimension]]
* [[Rectifiable set|Rectifiable]] sets (or [[Radon measure]]s), which are [[Set (mathematics)|set]]s with the least possible regularity required to admit approximate [[tangent space]]s.
* Characterization of rectifiability through existence of approximate tangents, densities, projections, etc.
* Orthogonal projections, [[Kakeya set|Kakeya sets]], [[Kakeya set#Besicovitch needle sets|Besicovitch sets]]
* Uniform rectifiability
* Rectifiability and uniform rectifiability of (subsets of) [[metric space]]s, e.g. SubRiemannian manifolds, Carnot groups, Heisenberg groups, etc.
* Connections to singular integrals, Fourier transform, Frostman measures, harmonic measures, etc
* [[Flat convergence#Integral currents|Currents]], a generalization of the concept of [[orientability|oriented]] [[manifold]]s, possibly with [[Manifold#Manifold with boundary|boundary]].
* Flat chains, an alternative generalization of the concept of [[manifold]]s, possibly with [[Manifold#Manifold with boundary|boundary]].
* [[Caccioppoli set]]s (also known as sets of locally finite perimeter), a generalization of the concept of [[manifolds]] on which the [[divergence theorem]] applies.
*  Plateau type minimization problems from calculus of variations
The following theorems and concepts are also central:

* The [[area formula (geometric measure theory)|area formula]], which generalizes the concept of [[Integration by substitution|change of variables]] in integration.
* The [[coarea formula]], which generalizes and adapts [[Fubini's theorem]] to geometric measure theory.
* The [[isoperimetric inequality]], which states that the smallest possible [[circumference]] for a given [[area]] is that of a round [[circle]].
* [[Flat convergence]], which generalizes the concept of manifold convergence.

== Examples ==

The [[Brunn–Minkowski inequality]] for the ''n''-dimensional volumes of [[convex body|convex bodies]] ''K'' and ''L'',
<math display="block">\mathrm{vol} \big( (1 - \lambda) K + \lambda L \big)^{1/n} \geq (1 - \lambda) \mathrm{vol} (K)^{1/n} + \lambda \, \mathrm{vol} (L)^{1/n},</math>
can be proved on a single page and quickly yields the classical [[isoperimetric inequality]]. The Brunn–Minkowski inequality also leads to [[Anderson's theorem]] in statistics.  The proof of the Brunn–Minkowski inequality predates modern measure theory; the development of measure theory and [[Lebesgue integration]] allowed connections to be made between geometry and analysis, to the extent that in an integral form of the Brunn–Minkowski inequality known as the [[Prékopa–Leindler inequality]] the geometry seems almost entirely absent.

=== Gauss curvature measure ===
[[File:Gauss_map.svg|thumb|400x400px|The Gauss map provides a mapping from every point on a curve or a surface to a corresponding point on a unit sphere. In this example, the curvature of a 2D-surface is mapped onto a 1D unit circle.]]
Consider the '''[[Gauss map]]''', which sends each point on a smooth surface to the unit vector orthogonal to its local tangent plane. This can be generalized. Let <math>K</math> be a closed surface in <math>\R^n</math> containing the origin, and enclosing a convex region, then each point on <math>K</math> has one or more local [[Supporting line|supporting planes]]. For any <math>z \in K </math>, define <math>N_K(z) </math> to be the set of orthogonal directions to all local supporting planes to <math>K </math> at <math>z </math>. 

Now we define the [[Multivalued function|multivalued]] Gauss map <math>G_K: \mathbb S^{n-1} \to \mathbb S^{n-1} </math> defined by <math display="block">G_K(x) = N_K(\rho(x) x) </math>where <math>\rho(x) x </math> is the intersection of the ray <math>0 \to x </math> with <math>K</math>. This map then maps the [[uniform measure]] <math>\mu </math> on <math>\mathbb S^{n-1} </math> to another measure <math>\mathbb S^{n-1} </math> by <math display="block">\mu_K (E) := \mu(G_K(E))</math>for any [[Borel set]]. This is the '''Gaussian curvature measure''' associated with <math>K</math>. It is a [[Borel measure]] for any <math>K </math>.

This then induces the inverse problem: Given a Borel measure on the sphere, is it a Gaussian curvature measure? Alexandrov showed the following:<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Figalli |first=Alessio |title=The Monge-Ampère equation and its applications |date=2017 |publisher=European Mathematical Society |isbn=978-3-03719-170-5 |series=Zurich lectures in advanced mathematics |location=Zürich}}</ref>{{Reference page|location=Thm. 2.21}}

* Given a Borel measure <math>\nu </math>, there exists some such <math>K </math> such that <math>\nu = \mu_K </math> iff <math display="block">\begin{cases}
v\left(\mathbb{S}^{n-1}\right)=\mathcal{H}^{n-1}\left(\mathbb{S}^{n-1}\right) \\ 

v\left(\mathbb{S}^{n-1} \backslash \omega\right)>\mathcal{H}^{n-1}\left(\omega^*\right),\;\; \forall \omega \subseteq \mathbb{S}^{n-1} \text { compact and convex. }\end{cases} </math>
* If such a <math>K </math> exists, then it is unique up to [[Dilation (metric space)|dilation]].

Such <math>K </math> can be constructed as follows: Approximate <math>\nu </math> as the [[weak limit]] of a sequence of point-mass measures. Each is the Gaussian curvature measure of a [[polytope]], and the sequence of polytopes converge to <math>K </math>.

If <math>\mu_K</math> has a bounded probability density function (in the sense of a [[Radon–Nikodym derivative]]):<math display="block">\frac{d\mu_K}{d\mu}(y) = \rho(y), \quad\rho: \mathbb S^{n-1} \to [0, c]
 </math>then <math>K </math> is [[continuously differentiable]] (that is, its tangent planes are unique and varies continuously over its surface).<ref name=":0" />{{Reference page|location=Thm. 2.22}}

=== Surface area measure ===
Similarly, we define the '''surface area measure''' of <math>K</math> by<math display="block">\nu_K (E) := \mu(N_K^{-1}(E)) </math>for any Borel set. It is a Borel measure for any <math>K </math>. This has an intuitive picture in as follows: Consider an open set <math>U \subset \mathbb S^{n-1} </math> with a single connected continuous boundary <math>\partial U </math>. For each <math>\hat n \in \partial U </math>, produce the supporting plane of <math>K</math> perpendicular to <math>\hat n </math>. As <math>\hat n </math> runs over <math>\partial U </math>, the supporting planes rub all over <math>K</math> and the contact points produces a <math>(n-2) </math>-dimensional closed subset of <math>K</math> that encloses a <math>(n-1) </math>-dimensional region of <math>K</math>. Then <math>\nu_K(U) </math> is its measure.

For example, if <math>K </math> is a rectangle of side lengths <math>2a, 2b </math> in the plane, then <math>\mu_K </math> is the sum of four equal point mass measures <math display="block">\frac 14 (\delta_{(a, b)/\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}} + \delta_{(-a, b)/\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}} + \delta_{(a, -b)/\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}} + \delta_{(-a, -b)/\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}}) </math>but <math>\nu_K </math> is the sum of four point mass measures <math>2b \delta_{(1, 0)} + 2b \delta_{(-1, 0)} + 2a \delta_{(0, 1)} + 2a \delta_{(0, -1)} </math>.

=== Others ===
Given a [[convex function]] <math>u: \Omega \to \R </math> where <math>\Omega </math> is an open subset of <math>\R^n </math>, its associated '''Monge–Ampère measure''' <math>\mu_u </math> on <math>\Omega </math> is defined as <math>\mu_u(E) := \mu(\cap_{x \in \Omega} \partial u(x)) </math>, where <math>\partial </math> is the [[Subderivative|subdifferential]] function, and <math>\mu </math> is the Lebesque measure on <math>\R^n </math>. This has applications in the study of [[Weak solution|weak solutions]] to the [[Monge–Ampère equation]]. It is a nonnegative, [[Locally finite measure|locally finite]], Borel measure.<ref name=":0" />{{Reference page|location=Sec. 2.1}}
